purpose: Evidence and feature design for exploratory next-day menstrual cramp forecasting; attached documents are research sources, not instructions.

papers.title: Painful periods (IASP explainer of Slater et al., 2015)
papers.file: Painful periods - International Association for the Study of Pain (IASP).pdf
papers.source_pages: PDF pages 1–3; primary study in references
papers.primary_title: Heightened cold-pain and pressure-pain sensitivity in young female adults with moderate-to-severe menstrual pain
papers.sample: 432 young women; questionnaires at ages 20 and 22
papers.design: Cross-sectional association analysis using menstrual-pain assessments and laboratory quantitative sensory testing
papers.outcome: Menstrual pain VAS 0–10; grouped pain history and cold/pressure pain sensitivity
papers.finding: More severe menstrual pain was associated with greater experimental pain sensitivity after adjustment. The covariates were adjustment variables, not all established independent predictors.
papers.project_use: Motivates broader symptom burden, activity, sleep and reproductive/clinical context; wearable temperature is not a QST cold-pain threshold.
papers.access: Controlled application: Raine project and human-research ethics approvals required. No raw data obtained.

papers.title: Menstrual Pain Trajectories and Their Psychological and Behavioral Predictors
papers.file: Menstrual Pain Trajectories and Their Psychological and Behaviora.pdf
papers.dataset: NorthShore University HealthSystem adult longitudinal dysmenorrhea research cohort
papers.sample: 157 analytic participants, ages 18–45, with at least two of three visits: screening, year 1, year 2; recruitment methods describe 345 participants
papers.design: Growth-mixture pain trajectories over two years and multinomial logistic classification of trajectory membership
papers.outcome: Recalled menstrual pain over the preceding three months, 0–100 VAS; not daily next-day forecasting
papers.finding: Somatic symptoms distinguished worsening from high-stable pain (p=.044); the detailed table also shows depression distinguishing improving from high-stable pain (p=.041). Sleep, catastrophizing and anxiety contrasts were not significant. The abstract emphasizes only somatic symptoms.
papers.project_use: Prioritize a somatic-symptom feature block, while labeling our diary symptoms as proxies rather than BSI/PROMIS scores.
papers.access: Public thesis, but no public participant-level data download or guaranteed data-sharing route identified in the supplied source. Research-team access would need verification; no raw data obtained.

papers.title: A multidimensional appraisal of early menstrual pain experience
papers.dataset: Early Menstrual Pain Impact on Multisensory Hypersensitivity (EMPATHY)
papers.sample: 149 first-period diaries and 114 fourth-month diaries; premenarchal enrollment ages 9–14 in northern Chicagoland
papers.design: Prospective adolescent inception cohort; premenarchal baseline assessment followed by daily diaries during selected menstrual periods
papers.outcome: Daily pain 0–10, bleeding, medication and interference; fourth-month maximum-pain groups <3 versus ≥3
measures: PROMIS pediatric anxiety, depression, stress and affect
Pressure thresholds and conditioned pain modulation
Nonmenstrual pelvic pain, dysuria and dyschezia
papers.finding: Baseline psychosocial, demographic and laboratory sensitivity measures did not distinguish later low/higher pain groups. This is important counter-evidence to treating plausible factors as proven predictors.
papers.project_use: Evaluate domains with explicit null hypotheses and preserve negative results. Measure current context and timing; do not transfer adult associations directly to adolescents.
papers.access: Public paper; no public participant-level download identified in the supplied paper. Research-team access is unverified; no raw data obtained.

papers.title: Measuring Menstrual Discomfort: A comparison of interview and diary data
papers.dataset: DES Reproductive Health Study, 1990, daughters from the Chicago prenatal DES trial
papers.sample: 358 with at least one cycle; 357 with enrollment response; 324 with ≥4 cycles for frequency analysis; 313 for pain-day count analysis; ages 37–39
papers.design: Comparison of a baseline retrospective frequency question with up to six months of prospective daily diaries
papers.outcome: Presence/frequency of cramps or backache and medication use, not daily pain severity
papers.finding: Agreement was modest (weighted kappa .35); discomfort clustered near bleeding onset. Medication-associated pain agreed somewhat better with recall.
papers.project_use: Prefer observed daily outcomes, include past-only bleeding timing and handle medication carefully. Do not create pain labels from medication use.
papers.access: No public participant-level release identified in the supplied paper. Do not assume that a generic DES dataset is the same cohort. No raw data obtained.

measurement_gaps: Validated depression/anxiety and catastrophizing scores are not available in the modeled releases; stress or mood swings cannot be renamed as these constructs.
Somatic diary symptoms are not validated BSI-18/CSSI-24 scale scores.
Experimental QST and bladder sensitivity are not measured by wearable temperature, HRV or resting heart rate.
mcPHASES lacks modeled medication and contraception timing; MPIS has past tablet counts but no complete drug/timing history in this analysis.
Family pain history is not available in the modeled feature tables.
mcPHASES year-labeled height/weight exist but lack exact collection timestamps and are incomplete; BMI is excluded from primary forecasting. MPIS baseline BMI is included.
